Oar
OR
noun
From the Saxon ar, an oar; a long shaft with a broad blade, worked against the side of a vessel to drive her through the water by the strength of men.

Biblical Definition

The oar is man’s own strength applied to the sea. It is the tool of the calm and the tool of the desperate hour, and Scripture uses it for both. Ezekiel builds Tyre’s glory out of the finest timber in the world: “of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars” (Eze 27:6); and he ends by setting the whole trade ashore in mourning: “all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land” (Eze 27:29). The men who drove the commerce of the nations stand at last on the beach with empty hands. Jonah’s crew show what the oar is worth against the purpose of God: “nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them” (Jon 1:13). They pulled with everything in them to spare a man’s life, and the sea refused, because the LORD had appointed otherwise. The disciples knew the same labour when Christ “saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them” (Mar 6:48). And Isaiah promises a country where the oar is not needed at all: “wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby” (Isa 33:21) — the broad rivers of the glorious LORD, where no man rows.

Webster 1828 Definition

A long shaft with a broad blade, used to row or propel a vessel through the water.

expand to see more

OAR, an instrument for rowing boats; a piece of timber flat at one end and round at the other.

From the Saxon ar; it is worked against the vessel’s side to drive her forward.

Tyre’s oars were made of the oaks of Bashan — the best timber of the region (Eze 27:6).

“All that handle the oar” is the AV’s phrase for the rowing seamen (Eze 27:29).

Isaiah’s city of God has broad rivers where no galley with oars shall go (Isa 33:21).

Key Scripture

Eze 27:6 — "Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim."

Eze 27:29 — "And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land;"

Jon 1:13 — "Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them."

Isa 33:21 — "But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby."

Modern Corruption

A plain implement made a standing figure of human effort — honourable in its place, useless against the will of God.

expand to see more

The oar is the perfect emblem of the religion of works. It is not wicked; it is honest labour, and Scripture never sneers at it. But it has a limit, and the limit is absolute: when the sea works against a man, he may row hard and he cannot land. Jonah’s sailors are the picture. They did not want to throw the prophet over; they pulled for the shore with everything they had, and the water fought them back, because the LORD had determined that this man should go into the deep. Every attempt to save oneself by effort ends on that verse. The moralist rows hard. The religious man rows hard. The self-reformer rows hard. And the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them — for no man can bring his own vessel to land against the settled purpose of God, and the only deliverance is the one God Himself appoints.

There is honour in the oar all the same, and the gospel does not abolish labour; it re-orders it. Christ saw His own disciples toiling in rowing against a contrary wind, and He did not rebuke the rowing — He came to them on the water. The Christian pulls at his duties, his callings, his family, his mortification of sin, and pulls hard; but he pulls knowing that arrival is not the fruit of his stroke. Isaiah names the end of the matter: a place of broad rivers and streams where no galley with oars shall go, because the LORD is our judge, our lawgiver, and our king, and He will save us. Heaven has no rowing benches. The labour of the saints ceases where their salvation always rested — not on the oar, but on Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the rowing-shaft by which men drive a vessel through the water.

expand to see more

Oar — Saxon ar, the rowing implement of a boat or galley.

Tyre’s were cut from the oaks of Bashan, the strongest timber of the land (Eze 27:6).

“All that handle the oar” is the AV’s name for the rowing crew (Eze 27:29).

Jonah’s mariners rowed hard and could not land — effort against decree (Jon 1:13).

In Isaiah’s city of God no galley with oars passes at all (Isa 33:21).

Usage

"The men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not."

"All that handle the oar shall come down from their ships and stand upon the land."

"No galley with oars goes on those broad rivers — heaven has no rowing benches."
